explanation: He answers from within, "Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee" (Luke 11:7).
hint: Picture a household already settled down for the night.

prompt: According to Jesus, why does the friend finally rise and give him as many as he needs?
options: Because he is his friend
Because he is paid for the bread
Because of the man's importunity
Because the children wake up hungry
explanation: Jesus says that though he will not rise because he is his friend, "yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth" (Luke 11:8).
hint: Jesus explicitly rules out friendship as the reason; consider the asker's persistence.

prompt: In his closing comparison with earthly fathers, what does Jesus say the heavenly Father will give to them that ask him?
options: Silver and gold
A sign from heaven
Victory over their enemies
The Holy Spirit
explanation: Jesus reasons that if earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, "how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" (Luke 11:13).
hint: Look at the very last verse of the passage.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: When the king's servants announced that the dinner was ready, how did some of the bidden guests respond?
options: They made light of it and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise
They said they had bought five yoke of oxen and had married a wife
They came to the wedding but left before the dinner was served
They asked the king to postpone the marriage until after the harvest
explanation: Matthew 22:5 says the bidden guests 'made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise,' even after being told all things were ready (Matthew 22:4).
hint: Think of ordinary daily business that pulled them away.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: When the king asked a guest how he came in without a wedding garment, how did the man respond?
options: He blamed the servants for bringing him in from the highways
He was speechless
He said he was too poor to buy one
He begged the king for forgiveness
explanation: Matthew 22:12 records the king's question, 'Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?' and states simply, 'And he was speechless.'
hint: The man offered no excuse at all.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: With what closing statement does Jesus sum up the parable?
options: So the last shall be first, and the first last
Whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased
For many are called, but few are chosen
The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few
explanation: Jesus ends the parable in Matthew 22:14 with the words, 'For many are called, but few are chosen.'
hint: The saying contrasts an invitation with a selection.

parable_title: The Marriage of the King's Son
prompt: Immediately after this parable, what did the Pharisees do?
options: They believed on Him and were baptized
They went away and held a feast of their own
They asked Him to explain the parable privately
They took counsel how they might entangle Him in His talk
explanation: Matthew 22:15 says, 'Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk,' leading to their question about tribute to Caesar.
hint: Read the very next verse after the parable ends; their response was hostile.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: In the first parable, what did the man do after he found the treasure hid in a field?
options: He hid it, then for joy sold all that he had and bought the field
He dug it up at once and carried it away by night
He reported it to the owner of the field and asked for a reward
He divided it among his neighbours
explanation: Matthew 13:44 says that when the man found the treasure he hid it, and for joy went and sold all that he had and bought that field.
hint: He did not take the treasure right away. Think about what he needed to own first.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: What did the merchant man, who was seeking goodly pearls, do when he found one pearl of great price?
options: He went and sold all that he had, and bought it
He traded it for many smaller pearls
He gave it to the king as a gift
He left it, because he could not afford it
explanation: Matthew 13:46 says that when the merchant found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
hint: His response is like that of the man in the field.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: In explaining the parable of the net, whom does Jesus say will come forth at the end of the world to sever the wicked from among the just?
options: The angels
The fishermen of Galilee
The scribes and Pharisees
The disciples
explanation: Jesus says in Matthew 13:49 that at the end of the world the angels shall come forth and sever the wicked from among the just.
hint: Jesus names the ones who do the sorting. They are not human.

parable_title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
prompt: After asking his disciples whether they had understood all these things, Jesus said that every scribe instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like what?
options: A householder who brings forth out of his treasure things new and old
A merchant who sells all his pearls for a field
A fisherman who casts away every fish he catches
A man who hides his treasure so that no one may find it
explanation: After the disciples answered 'Yea, Lord,' Jesus said in Matthew 13:52 that every instructed scribe is like a householder who brings forth out of his treasure things new and old.
hint: This picture also involves treasure, but instead of hiding it, the man brings things forth out of it.

prompt: How does Jesus describe the judge in this parable?
options: He feared not God, neither regarded man
He was a righteous man who feared God
He was a priest who served in the temple
He was the widow's own brother
explanation: Luke 18:2 says there was in a city a judge "which feared not God, neither regarded man." He had no reverence for God and no concern for people.
hint: Jesus describes his attitude toward both God and people, and neither is favorable.

prompt: When the judge finally decided to help the widow, what reason did he give within himself?
options: He had come to fear God
He wanted the people of the city to honor him
Her continual coming would weary him
The law of Moses commanded him to do it
explanation: In Luke 18:4-5 the judge admits he fears not God nor regards man, yet says, "because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me."
hint: His motive had nothing to do with God or justice; think about her persistence.

prompt: After saying "Hear what the unjust judge saith," what does Jesus declare God will do for his own elect who cry day and night unto him?
options: He will make them wait until they stop asking
He will avenge them speedily
He will give them riches and long life
He will send them to another judge
explanation: In Luke 18:7-8 Jesus asks, "shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him?" and answers, "I tell you that he will avenge them speedily."
hint: Jesus contrasts God with the unjust judge; consider how quickly God acts.

prompt: According to the narrator at the opening of the passage, to what end did Jesus speak this parable?
options: That men ought always to pray, and not to faint
That judges should fear God and regard man
That widows should not go to court
That men should sell all they have and give to the poor
explanation: Luke 18:1 states plainly that Jesus spake this parable "to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint."
hint: Look at the very first verse, before the story itself begins.

prompt: When the supper was prepared, what message did the man send his servant to give to those who had been invited?
options: Come; for all things are now ready.
The supper is delayed until the morning.
Bring a gift worthy of the master's table.
Only the first to arrive may enter.
explanation: The servant was sent at supper time to tell the invited guests, "Come; for all things are now ready" (Luke 14:17).
hint: The invitation stressed that nothing was left to prepare.

prompt: One invited guest did not even ask to be excused but simply said, "I cannot come." What reason did he give?
options: He had bought a piece of ground and had to go see it.
He had married a wife.
He had bought five yoke of oxen to prove them.
He had to bury his father.
explanation: The third guest said, "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come" (Luke 14:20), unlike the first two who asked to be excused.
hint: His excuse concerned a new household, not property or livestock.

prompt: How does the story close, stating what will happen to the men who were first invited?
options: They will be given seats of honour when they finally arrive.
They will be invited again to a second supper.
None of them shall taste of his supper.
They must pay for the food that was prepared.
explanation: After the lord orders his servant to compel guests from the highways and hedges so that his house may be filled, the story closes: "none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper" (Luke 14:24).
hint: Think about what the refusers lose by turning down the invitation.

prompt: In the parable the master sends for the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind. Just before the parable, what had Jesus told his host to do with a similar list of people?
options: Give them alms at the door but not seat them.
Call them when making a feast, for they cannot recompense him.
Send them away so that friends and rich neighbours may come.
Seat them in the lowest room at the table.
explanation: Jesus told the one who bade him, "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind," adding that he would be blessed because they cannot recompense him (Luke 14:13-14).
hint: Read the advice Jesus gave to the man who had invited him, just before verse 15.

prompt: In Jesus' story, how much did the two debtors owe the creditor?
options: One owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty
One owed a thousand talents, and the other a hundred
Each owed fifty pence
One owed ten pence, and the other one pence
explanation: Jesus said a certain creditor had two debtors: 'the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty' (Luke 7:41).
hint: The larger debt was ten times the smaller one.

prompt: When neither debtor had anything to pay, what did the creditor do?
options: He cast them both into prison
He forgave only the one who owed less
He frankly forgave them both
He gave them more time and demanded interest
explanation: Luke 7:42 says, 'when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both.'
hint: The creditor treated both debtors the same way.

prompt: Jesus asked Simon which debtor would love the creditor most. What did Simon answer, which Jesus said was rightly judged?
options: The one who had been forgiven least
Neither, since debts cannot produce love
Both would love him equally
The one to whom he forgave most
explanation: Simon answered, 'I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most,' and Jesus replied, 'Thou hast rightly judged' (Luke 7:43).
hint: Think about the size of each debt that was cancelled.

prompt: Turning to the woman, Jesus contrasted her actions with Simon's. Which courtesy did Jesus say Simon had not given Him when He entered the house?
options: He gave no bread for the meal
He gave no water for His feet
He gave no seat at the table
He gave no wine to drink
explanation: Jesus told Simon, 'thou gavest me no water for my feet: but she hath washed my feet with tears,' and likewise noted Simon gave no kiss and no oil (Luke 7:44-46).
hint: The woman supplied this lack with her tears.
